title: Prompt Caching as a Design Constraint

questions.prompt: Twenty turns into a task, you run `/model` to switch to a cheaper model. Your next message is one short sentence, but the turn is slow and expensive. Why?
options: The cheaper model is simply slower
Each model has its own cache, so the new model reprocesses the entire history as an uncached prefix
The message was longer than it looked
questions.explanation: Caches are per-model, so a switch means the whole conversation history is read with no cache hits, even though the content is unchanged. Option A confuses price with speed and misses the one-time spike. Option C is not a mechanism — `/model` does not trigger compaction. Option D cannot explain a jump of the whole history for a one-line message; the cost is the prefix, not the message.

questions.prompt: You edit `CLAUDE.md` mid-session and then ask Claude to follow the new line. It does not. What are the two accurate facts?
options: The edit invalidated the cache and applied immediately
The edit kept the cache and did not apply until `/clear`, `/compact`, or a restart
The edit neither kept nor invalidated the cache, and applied immediately
The edit invalidated the cache and did not apply until a restart
questions.explanation: Editing project memory keeps the cache — the file is held from session start and the edit does not rewrite history — but the new content does not reach the running session until a reload point. Option A gets the application right and the cache cost wrong. Option C gets the cache right and the application wrong. Option D inverts the cache fact: the edit is cache-safe precisely because it does not change the prefix.

questions.prompt: You are designing a long-running session. Which ordering best exploits prefix matching?
options: Put the most important instructions last, so Claude reads them most recently
Put stable content first and anything that changes every turn last
Reorder the context every turn so nothing becomes stale
Put the model switch in the middle of each task
questions.explanation: The API caches the exact matching start of each request, so stable content first and changing content last keeps the prefix intact. Option A is a good *reading* heuristic and a bad *caching* one — recency in the text does not beat recomputation. Option C guarantees a rebuild every turn. Option D is the mistake this lesson is about: a mid-task model switch invalidates everything behind it.

questions.prompt: Which of these actions keeps the cached prefix intact?
options: Invoking a skill that injects its instructions
Enabling a plugin that supplies MCP servers
questions.explanation: A skill's instructions are injected as a message at the end of the conversation, leaving the prefix unchanged. Option A replaces the history with a summary — a new prefix by design. Option B is a per-model cache miss. Option D changes the tool-definition layer when schemas load upfront, which sits at the front. The tempting one is `/compact`, which feels like a refresh but is a rebuild.
